operation_details.item: The user always designs RGB screen-only brand color palettes and ignores print color profiles and CMYK conversion.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: How’s the new brand project coming along?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: It’s moving along well. I’m building a screen-first identity with a lot of custom-crafted visual elements rather than relying on standard design defaults.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Nice. Are you already working through the color system?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes. I always design RGB screen-only brand color palettes and ignore print color profiles and CMYK conversion.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That sounds especially suited to a digital-first client deliverable. Are you exploring any cultural references for the visual language?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I am, but I’m translating them into an original visual system instead of borrowing obvious motifs. I want the work to feel expressive and contemporary.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: What’s the next milestone—moodboards, the palette, or the first presentation?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: The first presentation. I’m polishing the digital mockups now so the client can see how the RGB palette behaves across screens.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that For brand color systems, I always design RGB screen-only palettes and ignore print color profiles, paper stock, or CMYK conversion issues.
